  "narrative": "the first weekend of that month, i took the long route up the ridge alone after years of postponing it. the clear morning became cloud that hid the cairns, leaving me on wet rock with no idea which direction was down; i waited, ate my second sandwich, and repeatedly counted to a hundred. after an hour or so, the cloud thinned, and i followed fence posts to a track and the car, where i sat a long time before turning the key. i cannot file the day as good or bad: the hour on the rock was my loneliest in a decade, the view afterward was the finest i had ever seen, and i would not trade one for the other. the day taught me that waiting is a skill rather than a failure and that a frightening place can still be worth returning to; when i went back in autumn, the cairns were exactly where they had been all along."
}

  "narrative": "at about eleven, i borrowed a field guide to seashells and never returned it; it stayed on my shelf through two house moves and a university degree. every so often, seeing its spine made my face go hot, and i put something in front of it. in my late twenties, i returned it expecting a fine the size of a car payment, but the counter person said it had been written off and dropped it on a resale trolley, resolving fifteen years of minor dread in ten seconds. i acknowledge that keeping the book was nobody's doing but mine, and learned that the imagined penalty is almost always larger than the actual one. i tell the story at dinners because it is funny and so others carrying an overdue thing hear that the counter is kinder than the shelf, while remaining faintly ashamed of eleven-year-old me and faintly proud of the tote bag."
}

  "wound": "fifteen years of minor dread",

  "narrative": "at about eleven, i borrowed a field guide to seashells and never returned it; it stayed on my shelf through two house moves and a university degree. every so often, seeing the spine made my face go hot, and i hid it behind something. in my late twenties, i returned it to another branch expecting a fine the size of a car payment, but it had been written off, resolving fifteen years of minor dread in ten seconds. i acknowledge that keeping it was nobody's doing but mine, and learned that the imagined penalty is almost always larger than the real one and that imagining is the actual cost. i tell the story at dinners because it is funny and to let others carrying their own overdue thing hear that the counter is kinder than the shelf, while remaining faintly ashamed of eleven-year-old me and faintly proud of the tote bag."
}
